Unregistered charge and attachment in winding up

A government-owned chit company lent to a company and attached its properties under the Kerala Revenue Recovery Act. Its charge was never registered with the Registrar of Companies. When the borrower was wound up, the chit company asked for leave to continue the sale.

Does a lender with an unregistered charge, or with an attachment under a revenue recovery law, rank as a secured creditor in a winding up?

A charge not registered under section 125 of the Companies Act, 1956 is void against the liquidator and creditors. An attachment does not create a charge. A government company's dues are not government dues, so the lender was an unsecured creditor and the Companies Act prevailed.

Registering every charge with the Registrar (now section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013) remains essential. See the NCLAT's rulings in Volkswagen Finance and Home Kraft for how this plays out under the IBC.

Statutes: Companies Act, 1956, ss. 125, 446, 537; Companies Act, 2013, s. 77

First and second charge holders in liquidation

ICICI Bank held a first charge over a company's assets and another lender held a second charge. When the company was wound up, the second charge holder argued that section 529A of the Companies Act, which ranks secured creditors pari passu with workmen, also wiped out priority among secured creditors.

In a winding up, does a first charge holder keep its priority over a second charge holder?

Yes. Section 529A puts workmen's dues and secured creditors' dues on an equal footing, but it does not abolish the priority among secured creditors that comes from section 48 of the Transfer of Property Act and their contracts.

Lenders rely on this principle when arguing that charge priority should be respected in an IBC liquidation. The IBC's section 53 treats secured creditors who relinquish security as one class, and the NCLAT's rulings on pro-rata distribution (see Technology Development Board and later cases) are being tested in the Supreme Court.

Statutes: Companies Act, 1956, ss. 529, 529A; Transfer of Property Act, 1882, s. 48

Unregistered mortgage merged in a decree

Indian Bank obtained a mortgage decree (giving time to pay before sale) against a company. The mortgage had not been registered with the Registrar of Companies. When the company was wound up, the official liquidator asked the court to declare the decree void.

Is a mortgage decree void against the liquidator because the underlying charge was not registered?

It depends on the decree. If the decree keeps the unregistered charge alive, section 125 applies and it is void against the liquidator. If the time to pay under the decree has passed and what operates is an order for sale, the matter has passed from contract to judgment and the decree stands. On the facts the time to pay had expired before the liquidator applied, so the decree was valid.

A decree may protect a lender whose charge was not registered, but registration is the only safe course.

Statutes: Companies Act, 1956, s. 125; Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXIV
